::: {.why}
The divergence you plotted last night is the empirical definition of adverse selection, and it is the reason a market maker's problem is a statistical one rather than an operational one.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Report the post-trade mid drift conditional on trade direction and size, out to a stated horizon.
- Explain adverse selection in plain language and say how a market maker prices it in.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Quantify the drift: average signed mid move after a trade, as a function of horizon and of trade size relative to displayed depth. Report at 1, 10 and 60 seconds. The large-trade curve keeps rising, which is exactly the permanent impact from yesterday appearing conditionally.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Read Glosten and Milgrom's setup and note that their model produces a positive spread with no inventory costs and no processing costs at all, purely from the possibility that the counterparty is informed. That is the sharpest statement of why a spread exists.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Write the plain-language explanation you would give in an interview, in three sentences, followed by the sentence about how a market maker responds, which is by widening and by skewing rather than by refusing to trade.
:::
:::
